# Interview Transcript — the-board-on-the-wall

Source material for this piece. Per the Masthead flow, the draft traces back to this
transcript: every claim, number, story, quote, and detail in `draft.html` must appear here or be
cited in `sources.md`. Answers are recorded as spoken and deliberately NOT cleaned up — the
drafting step shapes them.

> **Demo piece — FICTIONAL.** Kestrel Bay Ferry Authority, its terminals, its people, and every
> quote below are invented for this repo. The speakers are characters, the clearances recorded in
> `sources.md` are part of the fiction, and nothing here reports a real event.

Roster run (3 of 11), **complete** — every persona's done-when checks are met:
**narrative-prober** (sequence with cause at each step, one throughline, the pivot told as a
scene), **stakes-prober** (what was on the line, the turning point as a scene), **layperson**
(every load-bearing term glossed in plain language).
Not used: architect, tactician, operator, customer-advocate, domain-specialist,
curious-generalist, polish-breaker, skeptic. partner-advocate dormant (no partner configured).

Consent note: the two speakers below are quoted by role, per `voice/demo-mira/style-guide.md`.
Clearance status for each is recorded in `sources.md`.

## narrative-prober  (done)

**Q1 — Take me back to the beginning. When did this actually start?**
"Well, the board started before me. It was on the wall at Terminal 4 — the back wall, by the
window, so in the summer the magnets were warm if you touched them. Forty years they said. I
started as a clerk and the board was already the thing you looked at before you looked at
anything else. Nobody introduced it to me. You walked in and you read it."

**Q2 — And what happened next? Why then?**
"The replacement was a scheduling system, and it had been coming for years — grant money, an
audit recommendation, the usual. What made it happen when it did was a retirement. The man who
kept the board was leaving, and the authority decided the knowledge should not leave with him.
That was the argument in the meeting, anyway. Get it out of his head and into a database."

**Q3 — Stop there — who was in the room, and what did they say?**
"The superintendent, the operations manager, two schedulers, and me taking notes. The
superintendent didn't argue against it. He said one thing, and I remember it because nobody
answered it. He said, 'Fine. But tell me who's allowed to move the red ones.' And the manager
said something about permissions and roles, and the superintendent said, 'Right. So tell me what
the system calls a yard day.' And nobody said anything for a bit."

**Q4 — So the story is really about a board becoming a database — is that right?**
"That's the shape of it. But the part I keep coming back to isn't the losing of the board, it's
the two weeks after, when everybody kept walking to that wall. Even the ones who had asked for
the system. They'd walk over and stand there, and then they'd laugh at themselves and go back to
a screen."

## stakes-prober  (done)

**Q1 — What were you actually afraid of there?**
"That we'd be slower and not know why. A schedule isn't a list of sailings, it's an argument
about who's where. Two boats, three crews, one that's always in the yard — that's what the
scheduler on the 06:40 used to say when somebody new asked how it worked. If you lose the thing
that held the argument together, you don't lose the data, you lose the reason the data looked
like that."

**Q2 — Was there a moment you thought it wouldn't work?**
"The third morning. A relief vessel came in early and the deckhand on duty needed to know whether
he was going out on the second sailing. He didn't have a login — deck crew never did, why would
they. So he walked to the wall. And there was a screen where the wall used to be, and it was
turned off, and the office was empty at 05:40. He came and found me. That was the moment. It
wasn't a system failure, it was a room failure. Everybody who needed the board could read it
from the doorway. Only some of them could log in."

**Q3 — What did it cost you — hours, sleep, credibility, a relationship?**
"Eleven days of it being slower, and I don't want to exaggerate that, because the system was
right and we knew it was right. What it cost me was that I was the one who had taken the notes in
the meeting. I had written down the superintendent's question about the red magnets, and I had
put it in the 'open items' column, and it stayed there. So when the deckhand came looking for me
at 05:40, I knew exactly whose fault it was, and it wasn't the vendor's."

**Q4 — Who else was affected, and were they told the truth at the time?**
"The deck crew, mostly. And the yard, because a yard day on the board was a chip in the magnet —
an actual chip, the red one had a piece missing from about 1998 — and in the system it was a
status code. The yard foreman asked me once whether we could print it out each morning and stick
it on the wall. We did that for a month. Everybody pretended it was a temporary measure. It
wasn't, and we all knew it wasn't."

## layperson  (done)

**Q1 — You said 'the red ones' — what is that, in a sentence my sister would get?**
"Colored magnets. Each color meant something. Blue was a boat on its normal rotation. Red was a
boat that couldn't sail — in the yard, or waiting on a survey. White was a crew change that
hadn't been settled yet, so it might move. Only the duty superintendent could move a red one,
because moving a red one meant telling somebody a boat wasn't coming."

**Q2 — What is a 'yard day'?**
"A day the vessel is in the maintenance yard instead of on the water. On the board it was the red
magnet with the chip in it, in the column for that day. So you could see it from across the room:
one boat out, and where the gap was."

**Q3 — Who was allowed to move a magnet, and what happened if the wrong person did?**
"Any scheduler could move a blue or a white. Only the duty superintendent could move a red, and
if you moved a red you said so out loud in the office, because it meant a sailing was changing.
That was the whole permission system. It was a rule about speech, not about access. If the wrong
person moved a red magnet, somebody would say 'who moved the Cormorant?' and you'd find out in
about ninety seconds."

**Q4 — What replaced it, and what did the replacement not do?**
"The system does everything the board did and more, and it's correct, and it keeps a record. What
it doesn't do is sit on a wall. You have to go to it, and you have to be allowed in. The board was
readable by anyone standing in the room, including somebody with salt on his jacket at 05:40 who
had never had and would never need a password."

**Q5 — Where is the board now?**
"They took it down in pieces. The superintendent kept the brass rail off the bottom of it — the
rail the magnets parked on overnight, so you could see at a glance how many were unassigned.
It's on a shelf in his office. He said, 'I could read it from the door.' That's all he said about
it. I don't think he was being sentimental. He was telling me what the rail was for."
